'''Ioan Mire Melik''', or '''Melic''' (born '''Iacob Ioan Miren Melik''';<ref name="lpsimtul">{{in lang|ro}} Liviu Papuc, [https://web.archive.org/web/20090308120238/http://convorbiri-literare.dntis.ro/PAPUCdec6.html "Ioan M. Melik sau simțul practic la Junimea"], in ''[[Convorbiri Literare]]'', December 2006</ref> August 9, 1840 – January 29, 1889), was a [[Wallachia]]n, later [[Romania]]n mathematician, educator and political figure, one of the early members of ''[[Junimea]]'' literary society. Known for his work in private education, and for his tenure at the [[Alexandru Ioan Cuza University|University of Iași]], he was the author of several early introductions to science—dealing with [[arithmetic]] and [[geometry]], but also with [[topography]] and [[surveying]]. He was perceived as a bland figure at ''Junimea'' meetings, and had little to do with its literary agenda, but took care of administrative chores and, for a while, of its publishing venture. In his other job as headmaster of ''Institutele-Unite'' high school, where he employed poet [[Mihai Eminescu]] as a German-language teacher, he was regarded as remarkably stern, and had a publicized showdown with the students.

Taking his cue from the ''Junimist'' leadership, Melik followed the literary club as it transformed itself into a [[Liberal conservatism|liberal conservative]] party. He represented [[Iași]] city in the [[Chamber of Deputies of Romania|Assembly of Deputies]] in the [[1884 Romanian general election|1884 legislature]], and then, under a ''Junimist'' government, helped enforce [[Titu Maiorescu]]'s policies in the educational field. Melik is also remembered as an engineer and entrepreneur, who contributed to the modern history of [[Răchiți|Costeștii Botoșanilor]] village, his personal estate. He died of an unspecified disease at age 48, and was survived by his son Eugen, who followed in his footsteps as both a politician and an academic. Melik Jr was a leader of the [[Democratic Nationalist Party (Romania)|Democratic Nationalist Party]] during and after World War I, but disappeared from public life after being exposed and sentenced as a confidence man.

==Biography==

===Early years===
The future scientist was born in [[Bucharest]], the Wallachian capital, on August 9, 1840 (although traditionally believed to have been born on August 15<ref name="lpsimtul"/> or August 21,<ref name="mdssocsec1">{{in lang|ro}} [[Mihai Dim. Sturdza]], [https://web.archive.org/web/20120424064233/http://convorbiri-literare.dntis.ro/STURDZAiun4.html "Junimea, societate secretă"], in ''[[Convorbiri Literare]]'', June 2004</ref> and wrongly credited in some documents as a "Iași native").<ref name="lpmasoneria">{{in lang|ro}} Liviu Papuc, [https://web.archive.org/web/20111206134341/http://www.sud-est.md/numere/20061123/article_8/ "Masoneria junimistă"], in ''[[Revista Sud-Est]]'', Issue 4/2006</ref> He was of [[Armenians in Romania|Armenian]] origins: the Meliks traced their origin to Ohan, a [[Armenian Apostolic Church|Gregorian Armenian]] clergyman.<ref name="lpsimtul"/> As reported by the mathematician's son Eugen, they were recent immigrants from the [[Ottoman Empire]], who had been scattered across the continents by [[Armenians in the Ottoman Empire|mounting persecutions against their community]]; [[Boghos Yousefian]], the [[Minister of Foreign Affairs (Egypt)|Foreign Minister]] of [[Ottoman Egypt]], was a close relative of the clan.<ref name="emscrisori">Eugen Melic, "Scrisori și hârtii vechi", in ''[[Adevărul Literar și Artistic]]'', February 16, 1936, p. 4</ref> Ioan's parents were Ohan's son, Arakel "Popovici" Melik, and his wife Maria Gedik; they had two other children: Gavril, a boy, and Anika, a girl.<ref name="lpsimtul"/> Ohan's other son, [[Iacob Melic]], was a successful architect. The Ottoman statesman [[Mustafa Reshid Pasha]] recommended his work to the Wallachian government, but Iacob left the country and settled in [[Paris]].<ref>Iorga, p. 92</ref> From his new home, Iacob Melik corresponded with the exiled leaders of the [[Wallachian Revolution of 1848|1848 Revolution]], in particular the moderate and pro-Ottoman faction of [[Ion Ghica]], [[Alexandru G. Golescu]] and Nicolae Pleșoianu.<ref>Iorga, pp. 92–95</ref> 

To the end of his life, Ioan was listed as having "Armenian Gregorian nationality".<ref name="mlkcurierul">"†I. M. Melik Profesor la Universitatea din Iași", in ''Curierul. Foaea Intereselor Generale'', February 1 (13), 1889, p. 3</ref> According to his own testimony, he first attended the Armenian School in Bucharest's [[Sectors of Bucharest|Yellow District]], and then regular school in that same neighborhood.<ref name="lpsimtul"/> From 1854 to 1856, he completed secondary school at the [[Saint Sava College]] and was, in his own account, an award-winning student.<ref name="lpsimtul"/> From 1856, Iacob Melik took over the boy's education, taking him to [[Second French Empire|Imperial France]]. Young Melik was tutored at a private boarding house (1857), before enlisting at the [[University of Paris]] Medical School, but changed his mind and applied for the ''[[Mines ParisTech|École des Mines de Paris]]'' (1860).<ref name="lpsimtul"/> He finished school in 1864, and worked for a short while at [[salt mine]]s in France and [[Belgium]].<ref name="lpsimtul"/>

Melik's work took him to [[Moldavia]], which, in 1859, had federated with Wallachia into the [[United Principalities]]. The regime of ''[[Domnitor]]'' [[Alexandru Ioan Cuza]] assigned him to inspect the Moldavian salt mines, at [[Slănic-Moldova|Slănic]] and [[Târgu Ocna]].<ref name="lpsimtul"/> Known to his Iași colleagues and friends as ''Mirmilic'',<ref name="gc440">Călinescu, p. 440</ref> he began attending the ''Junimea'' club in 1865, being one of the outside sympathizers of the cause, and manifestly lacking literary ambitions. [[Iacob Negruzzi]], the ''Junimea'' co-founder and biographer of its members, asserted: "[Melik was] once a passionate ''Junimist'', but always kept silent."<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="ccfarmecul2">{{in lang|ro}} Constantin Coroiu, [https://web.archive.org/web/20140714160440/http://convorbiri-literare.dntis.ro/COROIUsep8.html "Farmecul discret al documentului (II)"], in ''[[Convorbiri Literare]]'', September 2008</ref> Negruzzi jokingly added that the standard estimate, according to which the maths teacher had uttered some 23 words at club meetings held between 1865 and 1880, was probably exaggerated in Melik's favor.<ref name="ccfarmecul2"/> Literary historian [[George Călinescu]] suggests that Melik, like astronomer [[Niculae Culianu]] or schoolteacher [[Pavel Paicu]], only came to ''Junimea'' "out of devotion or for the sake of entertainment".<ref>Călinescu, pp. 439–440</ref> The mathematician was notorious for not having published a single line in the ''Junimist'' tribune, ''[[Convorbiri Literare]]''.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="gc440"/><ref name="ccfarmecul2"/><ref name="adxistoriaideilor">[[A. D. Xenopol]], [[I. E. Torouțiu]], [http://ro.wikisource.org/wiki/Istoria_ideilor_mele ''Istoria ideilor mele''] ([[Wikisource]] version of the 1933 print)</ref>

===''Junimist'' projects===
With his ''Junimist'' credentials, Melik was made substitute Professor of Mathematics at Iași University (February 23, 1865).<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="gc440"/> In parallel, he taught at a high school for young cadets.<ref name="mlkcurierul"/> During October 1865, he joined a group of academics, also comprising Rector [[Titu Maiorescu]], museum organizer [[Gheorghe Panaiteanu Bardasare]], Culianu, and Negruzzi, in expressing support for Cuza's autonomous interpretation of [[Vassal and tributary states of the Ottoman Empire|Romanian vassalage]]—namely, his attitude toward the Ottoman overlords. Their [[open letter]] congratulated the ''Domnitor'' for not accepting to be scolded by [[List of Ottoman grand viziers|Grand Vizier]] [[Mehmed Fuad Pasha|Fuad]].<ref>N. Grigoraș, "Titu Maiorescu apărător al independenței", in ''[[Tribuna (Romania)|Tribuna]]'', Vol. XI, Issue 18, May 1967, p. 6</ref> Melik acquired university tenure in April 1866, shortly after Cuza's regime had been toppled by the "[[monstrous coalition]]" and replaced by a [[Princely Lieutenancy of Romania (1866)|Princely Lieutenancy]].<ref name="lpsimtul"/> In May, he was caught up in the riots at Iași, whereby the [[Free and Independent Faction]] signaled its opposition to a proposed naturalization of [[History of the Jews in Romania|resident Jews]]. In a letter to ''[[Românul]]'', Melik explained that he did not support the Factionalist platform, but had merely objected to the riots being quashed by the [[Romanian Land Forces]], which reportedly ignored [[academic freedom]]. His protest against the arrest of a university colleague resulted in his temporary arrest, ending when the rectorate intervened in his favor.<ref>I. M. Melik, "Domnule redactore", in ''[[Românul|Romanulu]]'', June 2, 1866, pp. 32–33</ref>

Soon after, Melik became a conservative ally of the ''Junimist'' Rector Maiorescu, helping him do battle with the University's well connected Factionalists and the other [[Liberalism and radicalism in Romania|left-liberal groups]]. As noted by Călinescu, the University's ''Junimist'' circle was formed around Professors Melik, Culianu, I. Negruzzi, [[Ioan Caragiani]] and [[Nicolae Mandrea]], with ''Junimea'' itself being "a political get-together with some cultural aspects."<ref>Călinescu, pp. 399–400</ref> Although still recognized as a secondary and inactive participant, Melik was involved on several early ''Junimist'' projects, and referred to by Maiorescu as the group's "banker".<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="ccfarmecul2"/> In addition to promoting ''Junimist'' goals at University, he participated in founding (and financing) the club's own private school, or "Academic Institute". He himself described the event as follows: "In summer 1866, I have founded the Academic Institute, in partnership with several colleagues, from both University and High School [that is, the National High School Iași]."<ref name="lpsimtul"/> Melik took personal care about furnishing the Institute, purchasing its books from prestigious companies such as [[Hachette (publisher)|Hachette]], and keeping score of the more reliable publishing houses in Moldavia and Wallachia.<ref name="lpsimtul"/>

The institution itself left a mark on [[Education in Romania|Romanian educational history]], being seen as a model school in the field of private enterprise.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref>Vianu, pp. 32–33</ref> It remains primarily noted for its contribution in [[Humanities]], which were assigned to Maiorescu. [[Constantin Meissner]], the dedicated student and future ''Junimist'' pedagogue, recalled: "we [students] found ourselves speaking, gesticulating, moving our heads just like our precious model [Maiorescu]."<ref>Vianu, p. 33</ref> Another former student, and later teacher at the Institute, was scholar [[A. D. Xenopol]]. He describes his alma mater as "an eminent private school", and Melik as one of the "leading professorial forces" in Moldavia; he also credits Melik's "complete and measured exactitude" as influential for his own work ethic.<ref name="adxistoriaideilor"/> According to Xenopol, Melik's refusal to tolerate staff truancy earned him a reputation as a strict colleague. Referencing an Armenian stereotype, the other ''Junimists'' began calling Melik a ''mindirigiu'' ("[[quilter]]") of their absences.<ref name="adxistoriaideilor"/>

Melik was, with [[Vasile Pogor]] and [[Al. Farra]], a manager of the literary club's own publishing company—a bankrupt project, since Pogor would only purchase books from his own area of interest.<ref>Ornea (I), p. 28</ref> Before going down, this commercial branch of ''Junimea'' put out a number of general education works, including Melik's textbook ''Elemente de aritmetică'' ("Elements of Arithmetic").<ref>{{in lang|ro}} Richard Constantinescu, [https://web.archive.org/web/20140714230409/http://astra.iasi.roedu.net/pdf/nr55p31-32.pdf "Doctorul Anastasie Fătu despre ''Societatea Junimea''"], in ''Revista Română'' ([[Asociația Transilvană pentru Literatura Română și Cultura Poporului Român|ASTRA]]), Issue 1/2009, p. 32; Gheorghe Manolache, [https://web.archive.org/web/20140714130049/http://www.revistatransilvania.ro/arhiva/2005/pdf/numarul10-11/art9_literaritate_si_literalitate_sau_arta_de_a_traduce_pe_schiller.pdf "Sub patronajul Junimii din Iași (1863–1874). Literaritate și literalitate sau arta de a traduce pe Schiller"], in ''Transilvania'', Issues 10-11/2005, p. 24; Vianu, p. 8</ref> Melik was also a [[cashier]] during ''Junimea'' anniversaries.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="ccfarmecul2"/> Witnessing the decline of ''Junimist'' capital, he even proposed, unsuccessfully, that the club fortunes be invested in a salt mine.<ref name="lpsimtul"/> Melik was not dissuaded by the opposition, and continued to draft plans about investing ''Junimist'' money, forming a [[credit union]], and opening up the Humpel girls' institute.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="ccfarmecul2"/> His record of ''Junimea'' gains and expenses is seen by philologist Constantin Coroiu as evidence of Melik's "computer-like rigor".<ref name="ccfarmecul2"/> According to Negruzzi, Melik was an outstandingly passionate defender of Maiorescu's reputation. When the ''Junimist'' leader was framed a [[statutory rape]] scandal and taken to court, Melik provoked the judge to a duel, over not being allowed to enter the courthouse.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="ccfarmecul2"/>

===''Institutele-Unite'' and Assembly mandate===
On February 18, 1867, the ''Junimist'' mathematician was also admitted into the conservative wing of [[Freemasonry in Romania|Romanian Freemasonry]], or "Star of Romania" [[Masonic Lodge|Lodge]]. This branch of the [[Ancient and Primitive Rite|Oriental Rite of Memphis]] and the [[Grand Orient de France]], wherein Pogor himself had reached the 90th Degree, had for its Iorgu Sutzu as its Venerable Master, and came to include most of the ''Junimist'' notabilities.<ref name="mdssocsec1"/><ref name="lpmasoneria"/> On October 21 of the same year, Melik was granted the Fellow Craft Rank in Masonic orders.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="ccfarmecul2"/> Noting the role of ''Junimist'' Masons in combating the liberals' stated [[xenophobia]], researcher [[Mihai Dim. Sturdza]] suggests that the "Star of Romania" was in fact "a place of refuge, [...] where the foreign-born intellectuals [...] created a bloc with the conservative [[Boyars of Wallachia and Moldavia|boyars]] and the Jewish merchants".<ref name="mdssocsec1"/> Their main liberal detractors included senior academic [[Simion Bărnuțiu]] and other outspoken [[Antisemitism|antisemites]].<ref name="mdssocsec1"/><ref name="lpmasoneria"/>

Melik's 1867 arithmetic course was highly popular, going through ten reprints.<ref name="lpsimtul"/> He followed up with other textbooks and introductory courses: ''Despre moneta română'' ("On the Romanian Currency", 1868); ''Elemente de Geometrie'' ("Elements of Geometry", 1869, ten reprints); ''Elemente de Topografie'' ("Elements of [[Topography]]", 1879, four reprints).<ref name="lpsimtul"/> From 1883 to 1888, Melik, Culianu and [[Constantin Climescu]] put out the magazine ''Recreații Științifice'' ("Scientific Recreations"), considered a direct precursor of the more prestigious ''[[Gazeta Matematică]]''.<ref>{{in lang|ro}} Vasile Oproiu, [http://www.recreatiimatematice.ro/arhiva/12010/RM12010.pdf "Centenarul Seminarului Matematic ''A. Myller''"], in ''Recreații Matematice'', Issue 1/2010, p. 1</ref> The author continued his work at the Institute before and after 1875, when it merged with the "New High School" into the private-run ''Institutele-Unite'' ("Unified Institutes");<ref name="lpsimtul"/> according to the former student Eugeniu Vincler, the complete merger only took place in 1879.<ref>Vincler, p. 1</ref> 

Also in 1875, Melik formalized his adoption by Iași city, by beginning construction work on a townhouse (completed 1882).<ref name="lpsimtul"/> He married a local, Roxandra.<ref name="roxandra">Death announcement for Roxandra I. Melik, in ''[[Universul]]'', September 6, 1942, p. 2</ref> The new ''Domnitor'', [[Carol I of Romania|Carol I]], recognized Melik's educational merits by granting him the Bene Merenti medal 1st class.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref>{{in lang|ro}} [http://documente.bcucluj.ro/web/bibdigit/periodice/familia/1880/BCUCLUJ_FP_279290_1880_016_92.pdf "Sciri din Românía"], in ''[[Familia (literary magazine)|Familia]]'', Issue 92/1880, p. 576 (digitized by the [[Babeș-Bolyai University]] [http://documente.bcucluj.ro/ Transsylvanica Online Library])</ref> However, according to Vincler, he was a "stern" headmaster, and managed to alienate the students by bringing in [[Mihai Eminescu]] to serve as their tutor in German; they resented Eminescu because of his cantankerousness and his harsh grading of students.<ref>Vincler, ''passim''</ref> A small-scale student revolt, which involved future socialist agitators [[Constantin Mille]] and [[Vasile Morțun]], was curbed by Melik.<ref>Avramescu, pp. 285–287; Șuțu, pp. 208–209. See also Vincler, ''passim''</ref> According to one anecdotal account, he bent their will by ordering the cafeteria not to provide them with any food for the duration of their strike.<ref>Șuțu, pp. 208–209</ref> Reflecting back on his participation in the scandal, Vincler expressed shame, noting that Eminescu had since been discovered as a poetic genius, and elevated into the national pantheon.<ref>Vincler, p. 2</ref> Mille himself was spared expulsion after a personal interview with Melik, whom he knew, derisively, as ''Mustață-Roșie'' ("Red Mustache").<ref>Avramescu, p. 287</ref>

Melik was a distant witness to the [[Romanian War of Independence]] (1877–1878), which saw the country cut off her remaining ties of vassalage with the Ottoman monarchy; he collected the letters sent home by his relative, Captain Grigore Bănulescu, who had fought [[Siege of Plevna|at Plevna]].<ref>Dumitru Vacariu, "Războiul Independenței. Noi mărturii privind eroismul ostașilor români", in ''Cronica'', Issue 48/1977, p. 8</ref> Shortly after the establishment of the [[Kingdom of Romania|Romanian Kingdom]] in 1881, Melik also made his way into the ''Junimist'' political party. Maiorescu, who led ''Junimea'' members in and out of the opposition [[Conservative Party (Romania, 1880–1918)|Conservative Party]], assigned him a place on the independent list for Iași in the [[1884 Romanian general election|election of 1884]]. In practice, Melik, Pogor, Negruzzi and others were in a cartel with the ruling [[National Liberal Party (Romania, 1875)|National Liberals]], and were elected deputies on a united pro-government list.<ref>Ornea (I), pp. 298–299</ref> A while after, with [[Prime Minister of Romania|Premier]] [[Ion Brătianu]] ignoring repeated ''Junimist'' requests for cabinet positions, the entire faction moved back into the opposition.<ref>Ornea (I), pp. 299–302</ref> Carol I, the newly crowned [[King of Romania]], again rewarded Melik's services: in February 1884, ''[[Monitorul Oficial]]'' published news that the mathematician had been made Officer of the [[Order of the Star of Romania]]; when later [[errata]] informed Melik that he was merely a Knight of that company, he refused to accept the award altogether.<ref name="lpsimtul"/>

===Final appointments and death===
Melik had given up his position as headmaster in 1884, when Climescu took over.<ref>Șuțu, p. 208</ref> He was still an active popularizer on scientific topics, publishing, in 1885, a [[surveying]] and [[ballistics]] tract: ''Equerulu grafometru sau quadrantulu de campania al D-lui Colonel de Artilerie A. Costiescu'' ("The [[Graphometer]] or Campaign Quadrant of the Artillery Colonel A. Costiescu").<ref name="lpsimtul"/> In January 1886, ''[[România Liberă]]'' aired his polemic with the National Liberal [[Ministry of Education (Romania)|Education Minister]], [[Dimitrie Sturdza]]—he objected in particular to Sturdza's new grading system, which made students with one failing grade repeat the entire year.<ref>"Un conseil à M. Démètre Sturdza", in ''[[L'Indépendance Roumaine]]'', January 5/17, 1886, p. 1</ref> In 1888, Melik issued three new textbooks: Arithmetic for 3rd- and 4th-graders, Geometry for the primary course, and a ''Curs practic de Geometrie elementară'' ("Practical Course in Elementary Geometry").<ref name="lpsimtul"/> By then, he had invested his money into a large-scale agricultural venture, on the Moldavian estate of [[Răchiți|Costeștii Botoșanilor]]. The purchase took place in March 1885. As he himself noted, 507 ''[[Romanian units of measurement|fálce]]'' of land (some 726 [[hectare]]s) were exchanged for his 210,000 [[Romanian leu|lei]], cash.<ref name="lpsimtul"/> This was a third of the estate, as defined by tradition, and a half of the actual village.<ref name="efsmongr6">{{in lang|ro}} Elena Florica Șuster, [https://web.archive.org/web/20140714180248/http://www.araratonline.com/PDF/Ararat/2005/Ararat%2002%202005.pdf "O monografie meritorie"], in the [[Armenians in Romania|Armenian-Romanian]] community magazine [http://www.araratonline.com/ ''Ararat''], Issue 2/2005, p. 6</ref>

In March 1888, after prolonged political infighting, Carol I turned his back on both the Conservatives and the National Liberals. The ''Junimists'' experienced a moment of triumph, with [[Theodor Rosetti]] as Premier and Maiorescu as Education Minister. For a while, Melik himself was Secretary General of the Education Ministry, his position at the University filled in by [[Ion Ralet]].<ref name="lpsimtul"/> The ''Junimist'' loyalist was assigned by Maiorescu to inspect the Moldavian schools. Their common goal was to purge from the schooling system a new political threat: socialist activists. Melik was ordered to work only with the known anti-socialists, and to sack all those suspected of having affiliated with the socialist clubs.<ref name="ccfarmecul2"/><ref>Ornea (II), pp. 314–315</ref> In one such letter, the Minister instructs his subordinate to inquire about whether the known [[Marxism|Marxist]] [[Ioan Nădejde]] still had relatives working on a state salary.<ref name="ccfarmecul2"/>

In early 1889, still active as General Inspector of the Schools and Principal of ''Institutele-Unite'',<ref name="necrologe84">{{in lang|ro}} [http://documente.bcucluj.ro/web/bibdigit/periodice/familia/1889/BCUCLUJ_FP_279290_1889_025_7.pdf "Ce e nou? Necrológe"], in ''[[Familia (literary magazine)|Familia]]'', Issue 7/1889, p. 84 (digitized by the [[Babeș-Bolyai University]] [http://documente.bcucluj.ro/ Transsylvanica Online Library])</ref> Melik was struck down with a quickly progressing illness. He died in his home at Iași on January 29, and was buried with military honors at [[Eternitatea cemetery]]; despite his lifelong Gregorian faith, the funeral service was [[Romanian Orthodox Church|Romanian Orthodox]], delivered by the local ''[[Archiereus]]'', Irimia Galățanu, at the [[Annunciation Church, Iași|Annunciation Church]].<ref name="mlkcurierul"/> The ceremony was entirely sponsored by the education ministry, with a credit line of 1,500 lei.<ref>"Cronica locală. Credit extra-ordinar", in ''Curierul. Foaea Intereselor Generale'', July 16/28, 1889, p. 3</ref> His death was perceived as a tragedy by his fellow ''Junimists''. Poet [[Anton Naum]] wrote, shortly after the events, "We have lost poor Melik in the space of 7 days, however good and healthy he had been. It left me with a hallowed heart, seeing that we were very close."<ref name="lpsimtul"/> The same Naum took over Melik's job at the inspectorate, in March 1889.<ref>"Știri", in ''[[Universul]]'', March 3 (15), 1889, p. 3</ref>

==Legacy==
Melik's brief obituary in ''[[Familia (literary magazine)|Familia]]'' magazine informed readers that the inspector's schoolbooks had "genuine value";<ref name="necrologe84"/> a homage was rendered by ''Institutele-Unite'' in September 1891, upon its [[silver jubilee]].<ref>Șuțu, p. 210</ref> Later, the post-''Junimist'' historiographer [[I. E. Torouțiu]] presented Melik as a highly moral man of action: "He was one of the society's devoted members, without ever asking it for perks [or] advancements, even though he was in a position to demand them, under the governments of his political friends."<ref name="adxistoriaideilor"/> By 1978, when they were assigned entries in Ionel Maftei's dictionary of Iași-themed biographies, Melik and Naum were reportedly among the "picturesque and quite forgotten" subclass of ''Junimists''.<ref>Mircea Popa, "Un dicționar al personalităților ieșene", in ''Steaua'', Vol. XXIX, Issue 9, September 1978, p. 45</ref> 

The mathematician was survived by his widow and their four children, three of whom were daughters<ref name="mlkcurierul"/> (four other children had died in infancy).<ref name="lpsimtul"/> Roxandra remained active as a philanthropist, and by 1908 was serving on the board of Maria Hinna's ''Pînea Săracilor'' charity.<ref>"Informații", in ''Opinia'', March 7, 1908, p. 2</ref> One of her and Ioan's daughters became the wife of Lieutenant Colonel Nicu Scorțescu. A former student of her father, he served with distinction in World War I and died in 1924, while leading the [[Romanian Police]] in [[Hotin County]].<ref>Șuțu, pp. 390–392</ref> Ioan's only surviving son, Eugen, took over his papers.<ref name="lpsimtul"/><ref name="emscrisori"/> Himself a graduate of ''Institutele-Unite'',<ref>Șuțu, p. 204</ref> he was assigned as that school's headmaster in August 1898.<ref>"Ultime informații", in ''Opinia'', August 22, 1898, p. 3</ref> He then became a substitute Law Professor at the University of Iași, beginning in 1903. Unable to complete his Ph. D., and complaining about the criteria for academic advancement, he finally resigned in September 1920.<ref>E. I. Melik, "Criza profesorală la Universitatea de Iași", in ''[[Dimineața]]'', September 27, 1920, p. 6</ref> Melik Jr also built the towering landmark of Costeștii Botoșanilor, a castle-shaped vacation home;<ref name="efsmongr6"/> one half of the village is commonly known as ''Costești-Melic''.<ref name="efsmongr6"/> 

In parallel, Eugen became an establishment politician, serving as a Conservative deputy for [[Botoșani County]] in 1911.<ref>"Grandioasa sărbătorire a d-lui D. A. Grecianu. Banchetul Grupului Conservator", in ''[[Evenimentul]]'', April 14, 1911, p. 1</ref> During the conflict opposing [[Petre P. Carp]] and [[Virgil Arion]] to Maiorescu, he sided with the former two and their "neo-''Junimist''" faction.<ref>[[Theodor Rășcanu]], "Acțiunea noastră în Bulgaria. O rectificare și o complectare", in ''[[Vremea]]'', July 31, 1938, p. 2</ref> He finally defected to the National Liberal caucus in 1913.<ref>"Informații", in ''[[Evenimentul]]'', December 8, 1913, p. 2</ref> During the second half of World War I, when [[The Romanian Debacle|southern Romania under German occupation]], Melik was in Iași, which functioned as a provisional capital of the rump Romanian state. He joined [[Nicolae Iorga]] and [[A. C. Cuza]]'s [[Democratic Nationalist Party (Romania)|Democratic Nationalist Party]] (PND), and was designated a candidate for the Assembly in the scheduled elections of December 1918; his home also hosted the Committee for the Defense of Iași's Interests.<ref>"Informații", in ''Opinia'', December 21, 1918, p. 1</ref>

Upon the creation of [[Greater Romania]], Melik Jr had become general secretary of the PND.<ref>"Adunarea naționaliștilor-democrați de la Dolj", in ''[[Neamul Românesc]]'', October 6, 1921, p. 1</ref> His political career was cut short when he acquired infamy as a confidence man: in June 1924, the [[Ilfov County]] tribunal found him guilty of several counts of fraud, after he had illegally obtained control of a Bucharest townhouse from his late aunt Anika. Litigation over this issue, which resulted in Melik being imprisoned for eight months, was initiated by the [[Armenian Church, Bucharest|Armenian Church]], as one of the legal successors.<ref>"Ultima Oră. Un interesant proces penal. d. Eugen Melik condamnat la 8 luni închisoare", in ''Opinia'', June 28, 1924, p. 4</ref> In April 1932, he was again charged with fraud, due to his land speculation with Anika's estate in [[Tisău]], and was ordered to pay reparations to his victims.<ref>"D-l Eugen Melik condamnat pentru vinderea unei moșii ce nu-i aparținea", in ''[[Viitorul]]'', April 2, 1932, p. 3</ref> He was living in [[Botoșani]] in March 1940, witnessing there the death of his wife Elena; they had two daughters, Ioana and Nicolița.<ref>Death announcement for Elena Melik, in ''[[Universul]]'', March 27, 1940, p. 9</ref> His mother Roxandra died in August 1942, while in monastic seclusion at [[Agapia Monastery]], and was buried next to her husband, at Eternitatea.<ref name="roxandra"/>
